subject: physics
chapter_title: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter

concepts.title: Work Function and Electron Emission
concepts.definition: The metal surface grips its free electrons, and the smallest energy an electron must be handed to break out is the work function; heating, a strong electric field or suitable light can supply it.
concepts.key_idea: Different metals let go at different costs, and electron volts translate that cost into joules.
concepts.textbook_ref: leph203.txt section 11.2 (work function, electron volt, thermionic/field/photoelectric emission)
question_patterns: what is the work function of a metal and why do free electrons need it to escape
name the three ways electron emission can be driven out of a metal surface
how many joules make one electron volt
why does an illuminated zinc plate lose its negative charge
which metals answer to visible light in photoemission and which need ultraviolet
explain why particles from heated metals and from photoemission behave identically

solution_steps.explain: the electron is pulled back by the positive surface it leaves, so a minimum energy is needed
heat gives thermionic emission, a strong field gives field emission, and light gives photoelectric emission
one electron volt equals 1.602e-19 joule

concepts.title: Photon Energy of Radiation
concepts.definition: Radiation trades energy in whole packets: one packet, the photon, carries Planck's constant times the light frequency, and brighter beams just pack more packets.
concepts.key_idea: Photon energy depends on frequency alone, never on how bright the beam is.
concepts.textbook_ref: leph203.txt section 11.7 (E = h nu, photon picture points i-v)
question_patterns: find the energy of a photon of frequency 6e14 Hz
calculate the photon energy for light of frequency 5.4e14 Hz
what energy does one quantum of radiation at 1e15 Hz carry
determine E = h nu for a laser photon of known frequency
how much energy rides on a single photon of stated frequency
compute the quantum energy of monochromatic light at 7.2e14 Hz

solution_steps.explain: h = 6.63e-34 joule second
one quantum carries h times the frequency

concepts.title: Photon Count From Beam Power
concepts.definition: A beam's power is just its photon delivery rate: splitting the wattage by the energy of one photon gives how many photons leave the source each second.
concepts.key_idea: Photons per second scales with power once the per-photon energy is fixed by frequency.
concepts.textbook_ref: leph203.txt Example 11.1 (2 mW laser at 6e14 Hz giving 5e15 photons/s)
question_patterns: a laser emits 2 mW at 6e14 Hz; how many photons leave it per second
find the photon rate of a beam from its power and its frequency
calculate how many quanta per second a source of stated power delivers
determine the photons emitted each second when the per-photon energy and wattage are known
how many photons per second cross a target lit by a beam of given power and frequency
compute N as power over photon energy for a light source

solution_steps.explain: h = 6.63e-34 joule second
the quantum energy is h times the frequency
photons per second equals beam power over the per-photon energy

concepts.title: Photon Momentum
concepts.definition: A photon carries momentum as well as energy, and for radiation the momentum equals Planck's constant divided by the wavelength.
concepts.key_idea: Energy and momentum together brand the light quantum as a particle: the photon.
concepts.textbook_ref: leph203.txt section 11.7 (p = h nu / c = h / lambda) and Exercise 11.4
question_patterns: find the momentum of a photon of wavelength 632.8 nm
calculate h over lambda for a 488 nm laser photon
what momentum does one photon of a given wavelength carry
determine the momentum of an X-ray photon of known wavelength
how much momentum is packed into a photon of 500 nm light
compute the photon momentum from its wavelength

solution_steps.explain: h = 6.63e-34 joule second
photon momentum is h over the wavelength in metres

concepts.title: Einstein Photoelectric Equation for Kmax
concepts.definition: One electron swallows one photon whole: whatever energy the quantum carries beyond the work function shows up as kinetic energy, and the fastest electron takes all of it.
concepts.key_idea: Brighter light sends out more electrons, but only higher frequency makes each one faster.
question_patterns: find the maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons struck by 6e14 Hz light on a metal of work function 2.14 eV
calculate Kmax from the photon frequency and the work function in joules
what maximum kinetic energy do the emitted electrons carry when the photon energy beats the work function
determine the largest photoelectron energy for a 4.2 eV emitter under 8.2e14 Hz light
how much kinetic energy does the fastest electron get from one photon of known frequency
compute h nu minus phi0 for a photoemission setup in joules

solution_steps.explain: h = 6.63e-34 joule second
the quantum carries h times the frequency
the excess over the work function becomes kinetic energy

concepts.title: Threshold Frequency From Work Function
concepts.definition: Every emitter has a cut-off frequency: the photon must at least pay the work function, so the cheapest light that still frees electrons has frequency equal to the work function divided by Planck's constant.
concepts.key_idea: A bigger work function pushes the threshold higher, and nothing below it emits no matter the intensity.
concepts.textbook_ref: leph203.txt section 11.6 (Eq. 11.3 and Example 11.2 part a)
question_patterns: find the threshold frequency of a metal whose work function is 2.14 eV
calculate the cut-off frequency from a work function given in joules
what minimum frequency just manages to free electrons from a surface of stated work function
determine nu zero for caesium using phi0 over h
below which frequency does an emitter refuse to release electrons
compute the threshold frequency of a photosensitive surface of given work function

solution_steps.explain: h = 6.63e-34 joule second

solution_steps.action: divide the work function by it
solution_steps.explain: the cut-off satisfies h nu0 = phi0 exactly

concepts.title: Stopping Potential Prediction
concepts.definition: The retarding voltage that halts even the quickest photoelectrons equals the excess photon energy over the work function, shared out per unit electron charge.
concepts.key_idea: The stopping potential tracks frequency, not intensity, which is the decisive blow to the wave picture.
question_patterns: predict the cut-off voltage when 8.2e14 Hz light hits a metal of threshold 3.3e14 Hz
calculate the stopping potential from the incident frequency and the work function
what retarding potential halts the fastest photoelectrons for a stated frequency and emitter
determine V0 for a photoemission run with known frequency and work function
find the negative collector potential at which the photocurrent just dies out
compute the stopping voltage from the photon energy minus the escape cost, per electron charge

solution_steps.explain: e = 1.6e-19 coulomb
h = 6.63e-34 joule second
the quantum carries h times the frequency
only the surplus energy must be cancelled by the retarding field
the stopping potential is the surplus energy per unit charge

concepts.title: Kmax From the Stopping Potential
concepts.definition: The cut-off voltage is a direct energy meter: the retarding field that just stops the quickest electrons tells you their maximum kinetic energy as charge times that voltage.
concepts.key_idea: Whatever the emitter or the light, e times the stopping voltage is the fastest electron's energy.
question_patterns: the cut-off voltage reads 1.5 V; what maximum photoelectron energy does that mean in joules
find Kmax from a measured stopping potential
calculate the maximum kinetic energy as e times V0 for V0 = 0.6 V
what does a stopping potential of 2 V reveal about the fastest emitted electrons
determine the electron energy that a retarding potential just manages to cancel
convert a stopping potential into joules of maximum kinetic energy

solution_steps.explain: e = 1.6e-19 coulomb
the retarding potential times e equals the maximum kinetic energy

concepts.title: Wave Picture Fails for Photoemission
concepts.definition: If light were a smooth wave, brightness would set the electron energy and any colour would work given time; the actual threshold behaviour, intensity-independent energies and instant emission all contradict that.
concepts.key_idea: Only the one-photon-one-electron picture explains why Kmax ignores intensity and why emission waits for no one.
concepts.textbook_ref: leph203.txt section 11.5 (wave theory versus observations i-iv)
question_patterns: why does the wave theory fail to explain the photoelectric effect
why can no amount of faint red light eject electrons from zinc
how does the instant start of emission argue against continuous energy absorption
explain why the fastest electron does not speed up when the light gets brighter
what does the very existence of a threshold frequency contradict in the wave picture
state two wave-model predictions that photoemission experiments refute

solution_steps.explain: a wave should dump energy continuously, so brighter light should mean faster electrons and no cut-off colour
Kmax ignores intensity, emission needs nu above nu0, and the delay is under a nanosecond
one photon absorbed by one electron explains every observation at once

concepts.title: de Broglie Wavelength From Momentum
concepts.definition: Matter waves a wavelength of Planck's constant divided by the particle's momentum, so the more momentum a body carries the tinier its wave character becomes.
concepts.key_idea: The de Broglie relation welds a wave property to a particle property through h.
concepts.textbook_ref: leph203.txt section 11.8 (Eq. 11.5 and Example 11.3 part b)
question_patterns: find the de Broglie wavelength of a particle of momentum 4.9e-24 kg m/s
calculate h over p for a moving body of given momentum
what wavelength belongs to a matter wave of known momentum
determine the de Broglie wavelength from the momentum of the particle
compute the matter wavelength for a momentum of 4.5 kg m/s
how does the associated wavelength change as a particle's momentum grows

solution_steps.explain: h = 6.63e-34 joule second
the matter wavelength is h over the momentum

concepts.title: de Broglie Wavelength From Mass and Speed
concepts.definition: For a particle of mass m and speed v, first form the momentum m v and Planck's constant over it gives the matter wavelength; everyday objects end up with immeasurably short waves.
concepts.key_idea: Electron waves reach measurable sizes while a thrown ball's wavelength dwarfs nothing.
question_patterns: find the de Broglie wavelength of an electron moving at 5.4e6 m/s
calculate the matter wavelength of a 40 g bullet flying at 1000 m/s
what is the wavelength of a 60 g ball rolling at 1 m/s
determine h over m v for a dust particle of stated mass and drift speed
compute the de Broglie wavelength from mass and velocity
how short is the matter wave of a macroscopic object of given mass and speed

solution_steps.explain: momentum is mass times speed
h = 6.63e-34 joule second
the matter wavelength is h over m v

concepts.title: Planck Constant From the V0-nu Slope
concepts.definition: Plotting stopping potential against frequency draws a straight line of slope h over e, so multiplying the measured slope by the electron charge recovers Planck's constant.
concepts.key_idea: Millikan tried to topple Einstein's equation and instead measured h from its universal slope.
concepts.textbook_ref: leph203.txt section 11.6 (slope = h/e of the V0 versus nu line) and Exercise 11.5
question_patterns: the slope of cut-off voltage versus frequency is 4.12e-15 V s; find Planck's constant
calculate h from the slope of the V0 against nu curve using the electron charge
what value of h follows from a measured slope in volt seconds
determine Planck's constant from the straight-line photoelectric graph
compute h as the slope times the elementary charge
how do you extract h from the gradient of a stopping potential plot

solution_steps.explain: e = 1.6e-19 coulomb

solution_steps.action: multiply the slope by the charge
solution_steps.explain: the line's slope is h over e, so h is slope times e
